::: {.about-text}

Hi, I'm Shusuke Ioku, a Ph.D. candidate in Political Science at the University of Rochester. I work on political economy, combining formal theory with micro-level data—historical and contemporary—to study how technology reshapes political strategy, organized around three questions: what are the strategic implications of algorithmic technology and artificial intelligence, when does political competition turn violent, and how does government develop, broadly defined. In [recent work under review](research.qmd#verification-paper), I model how AI-powered influence operations degrade what online communities collectively know: identity verification screens out fabricated voices at the price of silencing the best-informed members, so an operation can deplete collective knowledge without deploying a single fake. Other projects examine how radical elites [broke interwar Japan's democracy through civic associations](research.qmd#fascist-paper) that circumvented parties and the military, how the accidental arrival of firearms in 1543 [remade territorial competition](research.qmd#military-paper) among warring rulers, how subjects' ability to [exit across competing rulers](research.qmd#exit-paper) disciplined extraction in Tokugawa Japan, why early medieval statebuilders [dismantled their own administrative apparatus](research.qmd#feudalism-paper) and set feudalism in motion, and how [hydraulic management](research.qmd#hydraulic-paper) shaped which early states endured.
